title: Gym Sets With Rest
story: Your coach hands you a workout card listing sets to do, each tagged with the muscle group it works: L for legs, C for chest, B for back, and so on. You do one thing per slot of time: either one set, or rest. You may do the sets in any order you like.

The coach has one rule: after a set for some muscle group, at least rest other slots must pass before you work that same group again. Those slots can be sets for other groups or plain rest. You want to finish the card in as few slots as possible.
task: Write fewestSlots(sets, rest). sets is a string of uppercase letters, one per set; equal letters are the same muscle group. Between two sets of the same group there must be at least rest other slots. Return the smallest total number of slots, counting rest slots, needed to do every set.
An empty card takes 0 slots. With rest = 0 there is no restriction.
constraints: sets contains only the letters A to Z

examples.explanation: One best order is L C _ L _ _ L, where _ is a rest slot. Every pair of L sets has 2 slots between them. The three L sets alone force this length: the first and last L are at least 2 × 3 = 6 slots apart, so at least 7 slots in total. The one C set fills a gap but cannot shorten it.
L C L C A B works with no rest at all: each L and each C has another group's set right after it. You can never beat 6, since there are 6 sets.

hints: In the first example, forget C for a moment and place only the three L sets. How many slots do they force, no matter what else is on the card?

The group with the most sets builds a frame. If it has m sets, they need m - 1 gaps of rest slots each between them. The other sets go into those gaps. What happens when another group has just as many sets as the biggest one?

Every group that ties for the most sets adds one slot at the very end of the frame. So the frame is (m - 1) × (rest + 1) + k, where k is the number of tied groups. When could the real answer be larger than the frame?

Count sets per group. Let m be the largest count and k how many groups have it. If the other sets overflow the gaps, you never need to rest at all, and the answer is just the number of sets. Return max(sets.length, (m - 1) × (rest + 1) + k).
bruteForce: Simulate slot by slot, and at each slot try every group that is allowed right now, plus resting, exploring all orders to find the shortest. The number of orders grows exponentially with the number of sets, so even 30 sets is out of reach.

A cheaper simulation picks, at each slot, the allowed group with the most sets left. That is correct, but it builds the whole schedule slot by slot, which is far more work than needed: the answer depends only on how many sets the busiest groups have.

js: * @param {string} sets  one muscle-group letter per set
* @param {number} rest  slots required between two sets of the same group
py: def fewest_slots(sets: str, rest: int) -> int:

tests.note: two groups tie for most sets: forgetting the tie gives 7
more sets than the frame: the frame alone gives 7
taking groups in alphabetical order gives 6

js: // The busiest group(s) build a frame; other sets fill its gaps.
py: tied = sum(1 for c in counts if c == most)
# The busiest group(s) build a frame; other sets fill its gaps.
walkthrough: The group with the most sets is the bottleneck. Lay its sets out as early as the rule allows, and you get a frame: m - 1 blocks of rest + 1 slots, then the last set. Groups tied for the most sets also need a slot after the last block. Every other set fits into the gaps, because each has fewer than m sets and can be spread across different blocks.
Trace "AAABBBCCD" with rest 1. Counts: A 3, B 3, C 2, D 1. So m = 3 and k = 2 (A and B tie).
• Frame: (3 - 1) × (1 + 1) + 2 = 6 slots: A B | A B | A B.

• C, C and D still need places. The frame has no empty slots left, but you can widen any block: A B C | A B C | A B D. Widening never breaks the rule, it only puts more slots between equal groups. To place leftovers safely, deal them one group at a time, one set per block, cycling through the blocks. Two sets of the same group then always land in different blocks, at least a whole block apart.
• No rest slots are needed, so the answer is the number of sets, 9. That is max(9, 6).

Two answers to keep apart: when the gaps are not filled, rests are unavoidable and the frame size is the answer; when the other sets overflow the gaps, you never rest, and the answer is simply the number of sets. The max covers both.
solution.timeWhy: One pass to count; at most 26 groups after that.
solution.spaceWhy: The counts table has at most 26 entries.
solution.takeaway: When a cooldown or spacing rule applies to repeated items, find the most frequent item: its copies set a lower bound, and everything else fills the gaps around them. Comparing that bound with the plain item count often gives the answer without building a schedule.
